title: Largest All-Ones Square
statement:
You get a grid of characters, each "0" or "1". Find the largest square block (same number of rows and columns, sides parallel to the grid) that contains only "1"s.

Return its area, the number of cells in it. If the grid has no "1", return 0.

examples.why: Rows 0–2, columns 2–4 form a 3 × 3 block of ones. No 4 × 4 block fits.
The ones only touch at a corner, so the biggest square is a single cell.
The whole grid is ones, but it is a 2 × 4 rectangle. The largest square inside is 2 × 2.

hints: Fix the bottom-right corner of a square. What is the biggest all-ones square that ends exactly at that cell?
A square of side k ending at (r, c) needs squares of side k − 1 ending at the cell above, the cell to the left and the cell diagonally up-left.
side[r][c] = 1 + min(side[r − 1][c], side[r][c − 1], side[r − 1][c − 1]) when the cell is "1", else 0. The answer is the largest side, squared.

explain.intuition:
Let side[r][c] be the side of the biggest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is cell (r, c). If the cell is "0", it is 0. Otherwise, look at the three neighbours that also lie inside any square ending here: above, left, and up-left.

A square of side k at (r, c) is exactly three overlapping squares of side k − 1 ending at those neighbours, plus the cell itself. So the square here can only be one bigger than the smallest of the three. The weakest neighbour limits the growth, like the shortest stave in a barrel.
steps: Make a table side the size of the grid, filled with 0.
Go through the cells row by row, left to right.
If the cell is "1": on the top row or left column, side = 1; otherwise side = 1 + min(up, left, upLeft).
pitfalls: Returning the side length instead of the area.
Using only two neighbours (up and left). Then an L-shape like the ring in the tests looks like a 2 × 2 square.
Comparing cells to the number 1 when they are the strings "1" and "0".

complexity.space: O(cols) with one row of the table

solutions.title: Grow a square from every cell
solutions.idea: From each top-left cell, keep extending the square while the new bottom row and right column are all ones.

solutions.title: Bottom-right corner DP
solutions.idea: The square ending at a cell is one bigger than the smallest square ending at its top, left and top-left neighbours. Only the previous row is needed.

followups: Count every all-ones square in the grid, of every size. How does the same table give that almost for free?
Find the largest all-ones rectangle instead. Why does this DP no longer work, and what does? (Hint: a histogram per row.)
